A comparative note on how foreign trade — exports, imports, and trade **policy** —
shaped industrialization in four follower economies. Citations appear as
right-margin sidenotes.

# Cross-country snapshot: tariffs on manufactures

Average ad-valorem tariff on manufactured goods [@bairoch1989; @orourke1999]:

| Year      | France            | Belgium | Germany     | United States |
|-----------|-------------------|---------|-------------|---------------|
| 1820s–30s | very high (prohib.)| low/open| fragmented  | 25–40%        |
| 1875      | 12–15%            | 9–10%   | 4–6%        | 40–50%        |
| 1913      | ~20%              | ~9%     | ~13%        | ~44%          |

Pattern: continental Europe liberalized 1860–1880, then partly reverted; the US
stayed protectionist throughout.

# France

*Role of trade: secondary to the domestic/luxury market; policy oscillated
between protection and a brief free-trade window* [@trebilcock1981].

* **Continental System (1806–1814):** Napoleon's blockade of British goods gave
  French cotton/iron temporary shelter but cut off colonial inputs (raw cotton,
  sugar) and export markets → mostly disruptive [@landes1969].
* **Protectionist era (1814–1860):** high/prohibitive duties on iron, textiles,
  coal protected established producers but kept costs high and slowed
  mechanization [@bairoch1989].
* **Cobden–Chevalier Treaty (1860):** with Britain — abolished import
  prohibitions, capped duties on manufactures at ~30% (later ~10–15%); triggered
  a most-favoured-nation treaty network across Europe. Free-trade peak
  [@kindleberger1975].
* **Méline Tariff (1892):** return to agricultural and industrial protection
  [@bairoch1989].
* **Export structure:** high-value goods — Lyon **silk**, wine, luxury textiles —
  rather than mass-produced staples [@trebilcock1981].
* **Outcome:** slower, gradual industrialization; per-capita industrialization
  lagged Britain and Belgium through the 19th c. [@pollard1981].

# Belgium

*Role of trade: central and decisive — the first industrialized economy on the
Continent, and export-dependent by necessity* [@pollard1981].

* **Early lead (1820s–1830s):** first continental country to mechanize coal,
  iron, textiles; **John Cockerill's** Seraing works (from 1817) became Europe's
  largest integrated iron/engineering complex [@milward1973].
* **Small home market → export orientation:** small population forced reliance on
  foreign demand for coal, iron, machinery, glass, woollens/linens
  [@trebilcock1981].
* **United Kingdom of the Netherlands (1815–1830):** access to Dutch colonial
  markets (esp. Java) boosted early textiles; **independence (1830)** forced a
  search for new markets [@milward1973].
* **Liberal trade policy:** generally low tariffs; an early, consistent
  free-trader after 1830 [@bairoch1989].
* **Trade infrastructure:** state-built **railway network from 1835** (Europe's
  first state system) and the port of **Antwerp** linked production to exports
  [@pollard1981].
* **Outcome:** by mid-century the highest per-capita industrial capacity on the
  Continent, second only to Britain [@bairoch1989].

# United States

*Role of trade: dual — raw-material exporter to Britain (South) and protected
infant-industry importer of technology and capital (North)* [@beckert2014].

* **Technology transfer (import side):** **Samuel Slater (1790)** reproduced
  British spinning machinery in Rhode Island; British capital and skilled
  migrants seeded New England textiles [@landes1969].
* **Cotton exports (export side):** raw cotton ≈ **60% of total US export value
  by 1860**; the US South supplied ~**75–80% of Britain's raw-cotton imports** by
  1860 — Lancashire's industrialization was tied to American slave-grown cotton
  [@beckert2014].
* **Protective tariffs:**
  * **Tariff of 1816** — first explicitly protective tariff.
  * **Tariff of 1828** ("Tariff of Abominations") — duties ~45–50%; provoked the
    Nullification Crisis.
  * **Morrill Tariff (1861)** and successors — sustained ~40–50% protection for
    Northern manufacturing [@bairoch1989].
* **Internal market integration:** **Erie Canal (1825)** and railroads cut
  internal transport costs, expanding the home market that tariffs reserved for
  domestic producers [@orourke1999].
* **Outcome:** trade financed and equipped early industry while protection
  sheltered the North; rapid catch-up, overtaking Britain in manufacturing output
  by the 1890s [@allen2009].

# Germany

*Role of trade: internal free trade first (customs union), external protection
later; export-led catch-up in heavy and "new" industries* [@henderson1959].

* **Zollverein (Customs Union, 1834):** abolished tariffs *among* German states;
  began with **18 states and ~23 million people**, expanding thereafter. Created
  a large internal free-trade market *before* unification (1871) — arguably the
  single most important trade event for German industrialization
  [@henderson1959].
* **Friedrich List (1841, *National System of Political Economy*):** intellectual
  case for **infant-industry protection** and railways; influenced follower
  economies broadly [@trebilcock1981].
* **Liberal interlude (1860s):** Prussia signed a Cobden–Chevalier-style treaty
  with France (1862), lowering external tariffs [@kindleberger1975].
* **Bismarck's tariff (1879):** the "marriage of **iron and rye**" — protection
  for heavy industry *and* agriculture; ended the free-trade phase
  [@bairoch1989].
* **Export structure:** late but rapid rise in **steel, chemicals (dyes/pharma),
  electrical engineering, machinery**; by 1900 Germany led world synthetic dyes
  and challenged Britain in steel [@trebilcock1981].
* **Outcome:** from fragmented and backward (1815) to the Continent's leading
  industrial power by 1913, with manufactured exports central to growth
  [@pollard1981].

# Synthesis: how trade mattered

* **Market size:** Belgium and Germany show two solutions to small/fragmented
  markets — *export orientation* (Belgium) and *customs union* (Zollverein).
* **Technology flows:** all four imported British techniques and skilled labour
  early (esp. US via Slater, Belgium via Cockerill).
* **Raw materials:** the US fed Britain's cotton industry while building its own
  behind tariffs — trade as both dependence and ladder [@beckert2014].
* **Policy spectrum:** free-trade Belgium ↔ protectionist US, with France and
  Germany swinging between; protection was the *norm* for catch-up economies
  (List's logic), free trade the exception (1860–1879) [@bairoch1989].

::: {.callout-note}
**On the numbers.** Tariff averages [@bairoch1989] are approximate ad-valorem
equivalents and vary by source/method; US cotton-export shares are from standard
trade series [@beckert2014]. Treat single-figure percentages as orders of
magnitude, not precise point estimates.
:::
